text: Installing Abhed. This video covers every supported path, from a single engineer's laptop to an enterprise deployment with no route to the internet at all.

Start with the shape of the deployment. Abhed is one static binary and one database. Around it, three things you choose: where the model runs, who signs people in, and how far the agent's sandbox reaches.

Three topologies cover the enterprise. Hosted, where Zybuu runs it for you. Private, in your own cloud or data centre. And air-gapped, where the bundle is carried in and nothing ever calls out. The binary and the guarantees are the same in all three.

What you need. A Linux or macOS host, a Postgres sixteen database, a model endpoint you control, and, for sign-in, either local accounts or your identity provider. Sizing is driven by the model, not by Abhed: the harness itself is a two-gigabyte container.
The quickest path is from source. Abhed builds with Go one point twenty-six into a single binary with three dependencies. Point it at a model, run abhed init, then abhed doctor.

abhed doctor is worth its ten seconds. It prints exactly what is in force: the provider, the sandbox tier, the store, the auth mode. Then it makes a real call and requires a real tool call back. A model that cannot emit one cannot drive an agent, and you find out now, not mid-task.

For a team, run the container. One script brings up Postgres and Abhed on a private network, with named volumes and no bind mounts to the host. The database is never published; Abhed is its only client.

The container is locked down by default: a non-root user, all capabilities dropped, a read-only root filesystem, no new privileges, memory, CPU and process limits, and a configuration mounted read-only, so the managed policy cannot be edited from inside.

Postgres is provisioned with two roles. A superuser used only to provision, and a plain application role that owns the tables. Abhed refuses to start as a superuser, because Postgres exempts one from row-level security, and row-level security is the tenant boundary.

Configuration is one JSON file. The model providers, the sandbox tier and egress policy, the store, the auth mode, absolute deny rules, and limits. Secrets never live in it: the database URL and API keys come from the environment.

Sign-in fits the organisation. Local accounts issued by an administrator, or OpenID Connect with Keycloak, Okta, Microsoft Entra I D, Auth0, or Google Workspace. Groups from the identity provider decide who administers. Registration is invite-only, never open.

For the air-gapped enclave, build a signed bundle on a connected machine: static binaries for four platforms, the vendored dependencies, the docs, the schema, a software bill of materials, checksums, and a detached signature.

Carry it in. On the target, verification is a separate step from installation, on purpose: the archive hash, the signature against your public key, and every file's checksum are checked first. A bundle that fails any of them never reaches the installer.
Then the same install, the same doctor, the same configuration, against the model served inside the enclave. Set the home link empty, so the console has nothing to point at that it cannot reach.

Day two is short. Add users, or connect the identity provider. Turn on OpenTelemetry export if you run a collector. Add scheduled runs. And upgrade by replacing one binary: the schema migrates itself on start, and every migration is idempotent.
One binary. One database. Three topologies. The same guarantees in every one. That is installing Abhed.
